title: Coil-built vase with flared rim
subtitle: An elegant tall coil vase with an outward-flaring lip in air-dry clay
excerpt: A coil-built vase about 22 cm tall narrows at the neck before opening into a wide flared rim. The walls are built from stacked coils of air-dry clay, blended smooth on the interior, and the exterior is left with a fine textured surface that shows the coil work. No kiln is needed. Once sealed, the vase works as a display vessel for dried flowers.
sourceNotes: Coil-building method derived from first principles. Historical coil vase form referenced from Encyclopedia Britannica 11th edition (1911) pottery entry. V&A open-access collection for comparative tall coil-vessel form reference.

glossaryTerms.definition: A rope of clay rolled to an even diameter, stacked in rings to build up the walls of a vessel
The joining method: roughen both clay surfaces with a needle, apply clay slip, then press together
The drying stage where clay is firm enough to hold its shape and be refined but still damp enough to accept added clay
Fully air-dried and unfired; lightweight, pale, and stable enough for surface sealing
Unfired clay in any stage of drying, from freshly formed to bone-dry

content.text: A tall coil vase about 22 cm high starts with a narrow base, widens through the body, narrows again at the neck, and opens outward into a flared rim 14 cm across. The form is built from
coils
of air-dry clay, stacked and blended over two or three sessions. No kiln is needed. The finished vase holds dried flowers or display branches: air-dry clay is not watertight, so it cannot hold water.

materials.name: Clay slip (same clay body thinned with water)
PVA glue diluted 50/50 with water (for sealing)

tools.name: Pottery calipers (to track diameter at each stage)
Banding wheel (for rotating the vase while building)

content.text: Preparation

Build this vase in three sessions: base and lower body (first session), mid-body and narrowing neck (second session after a two-hour rest), and the flared rim (third session after another rest). The profile changes direction three times: widens, narrows, then flares. Each change in direction requires the clay below it to be firm before the new direction can be sustained. Sketch the profile on paper before starting.
Making the base
Roll a slab to 8 mm thick. Cut a circle 10 cm in diameter for the base. Smooth the edges with a damp sponge and leave it to stiffen on the canvas for 20 minutes.
Building the lower body (widening section)
Roll coils to 15 mm diameter. Use the
score-and-slip
method to attach the first coil ring around the top perimeter of the base circle. Blend the interior of the join immediately with a wooden rib.

Place each subsequent coil ring very slightly wider than the one below, stepping outward by 3-4 mm per ring. This creates the widening profile of the lower body. After six rings the base should have expanded from 10 cm to about 14 cm in diameter.
Blend the interior after each ring is placed. Do not blend the exterior: leave the coil ridges showing on the outside for texture. Check the wall thickness after each ring: it should stay at 7-8 mm.
After six rings, cover with a cloth and allow the lower body to firm for two hours.
Building the mid-body (parallel section) and neck (narrowing)
Once the lower body is firm at
leather-hard
stage, add four more coil rings at the same diameter of 14 cm, keeping the walls parallel. This is the widest part of the vase body.

To begin the neck: place each new coil ring very slightly inside the previous one, stepping inward 4-5 mm per ring. After five rings the diameter should have narrowed from 14 cm to approximately 8 cm. The narrowing feels counterintuitive: the coil must be placed on the inner edge of the wall below and pressed inward.
The neck section is where the vase is most likely to buckle: do not add more than three rings of narrowing in one session. Cover and allow to firm for two hours after every three rings.
Forming the flared rim

Once the neck is firm, begin stepping each coil ring slightly outward again, as with the widening lower body, but now from the narrow neck diameter. After four or five rings the rim should reach 14 cm in diameter, the same width as the wide body section.
The final rim coil is blended smooth on both interior and exterior to create a clean, even lip. Press the lip between two damp fingers and draw the clay outward slightly to create a thin rolled edge.
The finished total height should be 21-22 cm. Use calipers to check the neck diameter and rim diameter against each other and against your profile sketch.
Drying
The vase is
greenware

from the moment it is formed until fully dry. Allow it to air-dry at room temperature with no direct heat or draught. Cover the rim loosely with a cloth for the first day: the flared rim is thin and will dry faster than the thick lower body, creating tension that can crack the neck join. After 24 hours, remove the cloth and allow the piece to continue drying uncovered. Full drying to
bone-dry
takes four to seven days for a vessel of this size.
Sealing and finishing

Apply two coats of 50/50 PVA and water, inside and out, allowing each coat to dry fully. A long-handled brush or a brush tied to a dowel reaches the interior base. For a natural look, leave the clay colour as-is after sealing. For a more finished surface, apply a wash of diluted acrylic paint (one part paint to four parts water) and wipe off with a cloth while wet: the colour stays in the coil ridges and gives depth to the exterior texture.
Use and care

This vase is for dried flowers, branches, or decorative stems. Air-dry clay is not watertight: do not add water. If stems need anchoring, fill the base of the vase with a ball of floral foam cut to fit the neck opening. Wipe the exterior with a dry cloth to dust. The flared rim is the thinnest part: avoid knocking or gripping the vase by the rim.
Variations
Make a companion shorter piece at 14 cm with the same profile: wide body, short narrow neck, small flared rim, for a two-vase grouping.
Use a wooden rib to blend the coil ridges on the outside. This gives a smoother finish. When the clay is leather-hard, use a needle tool to engrave a simple plant pattern around the surface.
Build the form in paper clay air-dry for added strength: the cellulose fibres help bridge the neck-to-rim transition, which is the most stress-prone area.
Troubleshooter

items.cause: The lower body was not firm enough to support the weight of the narrowing section, or too many narrowing coils were added in one session
items.fix: Stop building the moment the neck feels soft and wobbly. Cover and wait two hours. Never add more than three narrowing rings in one session

items.problem: Flared rim cracks at the point where it meets the neck
items.cause: The rim dried faster than the neck, creating a differential shrinkage crack at the transition
items.fix: Cover the rim with a damp cloth strip for the first 48 hours of drying. At leather-hard, press fresh slip into any crack and smooth

items.cause: Coils were not centred consistently during building, or the base was not level when the first coil was placed
items.fix: Check the base level before starting and use a banding wheel to rotate the vase and check the form from all angles as you build. At leather-hard, small leans can be corrected by gently pressing the taller side

items.problem: Interior coil joins are rough and visible
items.cause: The interior was not blended immediately after each ring was placed, or the clay dried too much before blending
items.fix: Blend the interior of every coil ring before adding the next one. Keep a damp cloth over the top ring while blending to stop it drying
